Analogue Disc

This page provides an overview of the workflow for transferring the three most common analogue disc formats found in the Library’s sound collections, Shellac, Vinyl and Lacquer.

Various factors, including physical degradation, can influence our ability to replay historical sound carriers so this information should be regarded as a general guide, with more complex issues addressed in accordance with best practices or in discussion with the Digitisation Manager

  1. Shellac
    • 1.1. Cleaning
    • 1.2. Replay Speed
  2. Vinyl
    • 2.1. Cleaning
    • 2.2. Replay Speed
  3. Lacquer
    • 3.1. Cleaning
    • 3.2. Replay Speed
  4. Best Copy Selection
  5. Stylus Selection

1. Shellac

Shellac discs are commonly composed of slate dust, natural resin, and other coarse materials, rendering them physically rigid but prone to chipping or breakage. The disc’s groove is a monophonic, coarsegroove.

1.1. Cleaning

Shellac discs should be cleaned on the Keith Monks disc cleaner using a mix of Photoflo and Deironised water:

Product Ratio
Photoflo 1
Deironised Water 70

1.2. Replay Speed

Replay speed is standardised at 78prm but other speeds such as 80rpm are not uncommon, especially for ealier acoustic recordings and non-european pressings. Where avaialble, check the disc label, the Sound And Moving Image (SAMI) catalogue or any releavant record label catalogues to confirm this information.

Non-standard replay speeds should be noted in the Tracking Database.

2. Vinyl

Vinyl discs are made of PVC, they are lighter and more flexible than shellac, and susceptible to warping if stored poorly. The groove is most typically microgroove, but early coarsegroove pressings do exist.

2.1. Cleaning

Vinyl disc should be cleaned on the Keith Monks disc cleaner using Industrial Methylated Spirits (IMS) and Deironised water:

Product Ratio
Industrial Methylated Spirits (IMS) 50
Deironised Water 50

2.2. Replay Speed

Replay speed is 33 1/3rpm for LPs and 45rpm for EPs/45s, but 78rpm discs and other variations do exist

3. Lacquer

Lacquer discs consist of a base-core typically made of aluminuim, although other materials such as glass, cardboard and zinc are not uncommon. The core is coated in a cellulose-nitrate or gellotine lacquer. The discs are physically ridgid and heavier to hold than vinyl and shellac (excluding those with a cardboard base). Lacquer discs are a high-preservation risk and suffer from severe degradation, including plasterciser separation and surface flaking.

Gellotine lacquer absorbs water on touch, so extreame care should be taken to identify the lacquer type before cleaning. The groove can either be coarsegroove or microgroove.

3.1. Cleaning

Cleaning a lacquer disc might not be possible if the surface degradation is severe, with cracked or flaked lacquer, exposing the bare-core. In this situation, if safe to do so, an inital transfer should be made and any signal from the disc retrieved before attempting remedial action.

It is vital to confirm the lacquer surface is not gellotine before attempting to clean the disc, as any contact with water or other cleaning fluids will result in detruction of the gellotine surface. The surface lacquer type can be confirmed by applying a small drop of water towards the disc’s centre, away from any grooved area, if the surface does not react to the water contact after several minutes it is cellulose-nitrate and safe to clean.

Where the intergity of the lacquer surface is stable, the disc should be cleaned in the ultra-sonic bath filled with Deironised water. Where the surface shows plasticizer exudation the disc should be manually cleaned with a mix of Ammonia, Lens Cleaner and Deironised water, this can be done on the Keith Monks platter for easier application and drying.

Product Ratio
Ammonia 1
Len Cleaner 5
Deironised Water 94

3.2. Replay Speed

The majority of lacquer discs are cut at a standard speed, reflective of the era in which they were produced. However, many lacquers within the Library’s collections are not professional studio productions. Consequently, the speed and cut of these lacquers may vary, depending on the quality of equipment used and the individual recordist’s knowledge and approach. It is important to check any data in SAMI or documentation to confirm, where possible, how the recordings were produced.

If uncertainties exist regarding the speed or any other technical parameters, it should be noted in the Tracking Database.

4. Best Copy Selection

The majority of shellac and vinyl discs in the Library’s collections are commercial publications, often with multiple copies available. When multiple copies exist, engineers should assess the condition of each disc and select the best one for transfer.

Visual inspection is the first step, identifying any obvious damage or defects. If copies are in similar condition, discs should then undergo cleaning, followed by an audio comparison to assess sound quality and groove condition.

Once the best copy has been determined, the shelfmark of the chosen disc should be noted in the Tracking Database

5. Stylus Selection

An appropriate stylus should be selected to extract the highest fidelity signal while minimising noise and signal distortion. Choosing the appropriate stylus will be influenced by the disc’s production, manufacture and its playback and storage history. Comparative listening tests between styli are essential to determine the most suitable stylus for transfer.

Size (mil) Tip (Eliptical / Conical) Groove Type
0.07 E Micro
1.1 E Micro
2.0 E/C Coarse
2.3 E/C Coarse
2.5 E/C Coarse
2.8 E/C Coarse
3.0 E/C Coarse
3.5 E/C Coarse
4.0 E/C Coarse

6. FLAT Transfer

All shellac, lacquer and non-standard vinyl should be transferred with a FLAT setting through the Eldberg pre-amp, with no de-emphasis applied to the signal. The only exception to this is commercial vinyl recorded with a standard RIAA pre-emphasis curve.

The FLAT transfer will be treated as the Archival Master file and named with a _v1 suffix, in-line with Library’s filenaming convention.

7. v2 Access Copy

For Access purposes a second version of the file should be created from the FLAT, v1 transfer.

The second version be should be processed in software to apply the appropriate de-emphasis curve and, where the original recording is mono, the two-channel transfer summed to produce a dual-mono file. The post-processing can be done in Brian Davies Equalizer or another tool of choice, such as Audacity’s Graphic Equalizer.

The second file version should be named in the same convention as the Archive Master but with a _v2 suffix.

Note, where a disc that has no pre-emphasis applied but the original is mono, a FLAT, dual-mono _v2 file should still be created for access.
